directAnswerTitle: What is physical AI data collection?

directAnswerBody.text: Physical AI data collection is the operational work of capturing real-world robot demonstrations and multi-sensor recordings that a model can actually learn from: teleoperated episodes, kinesthetic demonstrations, human video, and hybrid autonomous rollouts, each logged with camera views, joint states, force data, and task labels.

It's the layer that sits between "we have a robot and an idea for a foundation model" and "we have a dataset our training pipeline can consume." Skip it, or treat it as an afterthought, and even a well-designed model architecture has nothing reliable to learn from.

directAnswerChecklistTitle: You need this if you're building:

directAnswerChecklist.text: An imitation learning or VLA policy for a specific manipulation task
A generalist robot foundation model that needs broad task coverage
A fine-tune of an existing model (GR00T, π₀, OpenVLA) on your own hardware
An evaluation suite to benchmark policy performance before deployment

problemsTitle: The bottleneck in physical AI isn't compute. It's real-world data.
problemsDescription: Language models learned from a decade of internet text. Robots don't have that luxury — every demonstration of "pick up this part" or "fold this towel" has to be physically performed, recorded, and labeled by someone.

problems.title: Volume without diversity fails
problems.description: Datasets skew toward a handful of "head" tasks while rare "tail" tasks get only a few examples. Research on long-tail imitation learning shows policies degrade sharply on exactly those under-represented tasks — the ones most likely to show up in real deployments. Read the study.

problems.title: Curated beats large
problems.description: A well-curated set of roughly 500 demonstrations fine-tuning a 7B parameter model has been shown to outperform a poorly curated fine-tune of a 70B model on manipulation benchmarks. Quality control decides outcomes more than raw scale. Source: State of Robotics 2026.

problems.title: Nobody can do it alone
problems.description: Even large robotics labs are turning to outside data partners, because building internal data-collection infrastructure pulls engineering time away from model and hardware work. IBM's reporting on the data gap covers why this shift is happening industry-wide.

methodsTitle: Four ways to collect robot data. We pick the right mix for your task.
methodsDescription: No single method covers every task well. Most production datasets blend two or three of these, weighted by how contact-rich the task is and how much hardware access you have.

rows.bestFor: Precise manipulation, bimanual tasks, contact-rich actions
rows.fidelity: High — captures true robot action space

rows.methodSub: Physically guiding the arm through the task
rows.fidelity: High for the specific arm, low transferability
rows.scalability: Low — one demonstration at a time

rows.methodSub: No robot in the loop, first-person or fixed camera
rows.bestFor: Rapid task coverage, pretraining, rare scenarios
rows.fidelity: Lower — needs retargeting to robot embodiment

rows.bestFor: Scaling a model that already has baseline competence
rows.fidelity: Variable — depends on current policy quality
rows.scalability: High — reduces human time per episode

qualityDescription: Every delivered episode is scored across five dimensions before it enters your dataset. This is how we catch the failures that don't show up until a model is already training on bad data.

qualityList.title: Task success
qualityList.description: Did the episode actually achieve the stated goal, verified against defined success criteria — not just "did the arm move."

qualityList.title: Trajectory smoothness
qualityList.description: Flags jerky corrections and oscillation common in novice teleoperation, which quietly degrades policy learning.

qualityList.title: Calibration drift
qualityList.description: Camera and sensor calibration is checked against the session baseline so silent drift doesn't corrupt a batch.

qualityList.title: Annotation consistency
qualityList.description: Task boundaries, language labels, and episode metadata are checked against a shared standard across operators.

qualityList.title: Environment coverage
qualityList.description: Tracks lighting, object, and layout variation against your target diversity plan to avoid a narrow, overfit dataset.

qualityCardHtml:
Demonstration quality research shows that novice or end-user teleoperation tends to introduce unstable control and inconsistent execution that's invisible unless you're specifically measuring for it. See the underlying research on data quality metrics in imitation learning.

Consistency in how actions are labeled and recorded matters as much as the demonstrations themselves — it's one of the four pillars commonly cited for usable learning-from-demonstration data, alongside diversity, precision, and scalability.
pitfallsTitle: What most robotics teams get wrong about data collection

pitfalls.title: Treating it like generic crowdsourced labeling
pitfalls.description: Robot demonstration data isn't a static image with a bounding box. It's continuous motion where the start, end, and transition points of an action are ambiguous unless the person recording understands the task. Generic labeling workflows built for text or image annotation don't transfer cleanly. This distinction is where a lot of in-house pipelines quietly break down.

pitfalls.title: Letting operator fatigue erode consistency
pitfalls.description: Long, uncapped sessions produce more corrective motions and drift as operators tire. Industry practice among dedicated teleoperation providers caps sessions around 45 minutes specifically to protect data consistency. This is a documented operating pattern, not a guess.

pitfalls.title: Ignoring the long tail until deployment
pitfalls.description: It's tempting to collect whatever demonstrations are easy first. Then a model ships and fails exactly on the rare-but-important cases nobody prioritized recording. Planning tail-task coverage from the start costs less than fixing it after a failed deployment.

pitfalls.title: Skipping calibration logging
pitfalls.description: Camera and sensor calibration drifts over weeks of use. Without a logged baseline to compare against, a whole batch of otherwise-good demonstrations can silently degrade model performance and the cause is nearly impossible to trace after the fact.

costsTitle: What in-house data collection actually costs
costsIntro: Building this internally isn't just "buy a robot and record." Teams typically underestimate:

costs.text: Calibration rigs, multi-camera arrays, and haptic controllers for the collection cell itself
Hiring and qualifying teleoperators, plus ongoing operator management
Engineering time spent building — and maintaining — QA and format-conversion tooling
Storage and dataset-versioning infrastructure as episode counts scale

costsOutro: Outsourcing the operational layer lets your team spend its time on model architecture and policy evaluation instead of rig maintenance.

faqTitle: Common questions about data collection engagements

faqs.question: What is physical AI data collection?
faqs.answer: It's the process of capturing real-world robot demonstrations and sensor recordings — through teleoperation, kinesthetic teaching, or human video — structured into datasets that imitation learning, reinforcement learning, and VLA models can train on.

faqs.question: How much robot demonstration data do I actually need?
faqs.answer: There's no universal number. A carefully curated batch of around 500 demonstrations on a well-scoped task can outperform a much larger, poorly curated dataset. Task diversity and annotation consistency matter more than raw volume.

faqs.question: What's the difference between teleoperation, kinesthetic teaching, and human video?
faqs.answer: Teleoperation drives the robot remotely while it records its own state. Kinesthetic teaching means physically guiding the robot's arm. Human video captures a person doing the task with no robot involved, which is cheaper but needs extra work to map onto a robot's action space.

faqs.question: What data formats do you deliver?
faqs.answer: RLDS, HDF5, Zarr, and LeRobot-compatible structures, each with camera calibration, robot URDF, action-space documentation, and per-episode metadata included.

faqs.question: Which robots and hardware platforms are supported?
faqs.answer: Franka Emika Panda, UR5e, ViperX-based bimanual rigs, mobile manipulators, and humanoid platforms. Custom or proprietary hardware can be onboarded once calibration and safety requirements are scoped.

faqs.question: How is data quality checked before delivery?
faqs.answer: Every episode runs through our Episode Integrity Score across task success, trajectory smoothness, calibration drift, annotation consistency, and environment coverage, with borderline episodes routed to replay review.

faqs.question: Do you offer a pilot before a full data collection program?
faqs.answer: Yes. Engagements typically start with a scoped pilot on one or two tasks to validate the collection protocol and quality bar before scaling to ongoing weekly volumes.
